items.title: London to Tokyo flights cross Siberia — not because Russia is convenient
items.claim: On a flat map, the shortest path between London and Tokyo looks like a horizontal line through Central Asia. The ACTUAL shortest path on Earth's surface arcs north over Siberia. That's the great-circle route.
items.prompt: Why is the great-circle route shortest?

options.text: Any geodesic (shortest path) on a sphere is part of a great circle — a circle whose plane passes through the sphere's centre. Latitude lines (except the equator) are NOT great circles, so flying along a latitude isn't optimal

items.reveal:
A geodesic is the shortest path between two points on a surface. On a flat plane, geodesics are straight lines. On a sphere, geodesics are arcs of great circles — circles whose centre coincides with the sphere's centre.

All meridians (longitude lines, including the prime meridian and date line) are great circles. The equator is a great circle. Lines of latitude EXCEPT the equator are NOT great circles — they're small circles whose plane does not pass through Earth's centre.

London-Tokyo: separated by ~9600 km along the great-circle route, ~12000 km if you fly along the line of latitude (~50°N).

Map projections distort geodesics:
- Mercator projection (Gerardus Mercator, 1569): preserves angles (conformal), shows rhumb lines as straight, but distorts areas and great-circle paths.
- Gnomonic projection: shows great circles as straight lines, but is unsuitable as a navigational chart.
- Robinson, Mollweide: balance distortions in different ways.

Airlines plan routes along great circles, adjusted for winds (jetstream eastbound from US to Europe saves an hour). 'Polar' routes from North America to East Asia routinely cross the Arctic.

In general relativity, geodesics on curved spacetime trace the paths of free-falling objects — gravity IS geodesic motion through curved spacetime.
items.why: Maps lie about distances. Modern navigation requires understanding that the shortest path on a sphere is curved on a flat map. The intuition fails everywhere except locally.

items.title: Newton's biggest theorem says integration and differentiation are inverses
items.claim: Define F(x) as the area under f from 0 to x. The derivative of F is f. Define G(x) as an antiderivative of f. Then integral from a to b of f dx = G(b) - G(a). Two operations that look unrelated are inverses.

options.text: Integration (continuous summation) and differentiation (instantaneous rate) seem like different operations — but they undo each other. This is one of the most surprising and powerful results in mathematics

items.reveal:
Two parts:

FTC Part I: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).

FTC Part II: If f is continuous on [a, b] and G is any antiderivative of f (so G'(x) = f(x)), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a).

Geometric intuition for Part I: F(x) is area under the curve up to x. As x increases by a small amount dx, the area increases by approximately f(x) * dx — the height at x times the width dx. So dF/dx = f(x).

Why it's surprising:
- Differentiation computes a LOCAL rate at one point.
- Integration sums up TOTAL accumulated value across a range.
- The connection: knowing the total at every point tells you the rate; knowing the rate everywhere tells you the total.

Applications:
- Definite integrals become easy: find an antiderivative, plug in endpoints, subtract.
- Areas, volumes, work, charge, total amounts of accumulated quantities — all computable via antiderivatives.
- Differential equations: solving f' = g is equivalent to finding an antiderivative of g.

Historical: Newton (~1665) and Leibniz (~1675) both discovered it independently. It's the cornerstone of mathematical physics.

Before the FTC, calculating areas under curves (the 'quadrature problem') was a major mathematical challenge — Archimedes computed parabola areas through laborious limit arguments. After the FTC, antiderivatives reduce the problem to algebra.
items.why: Calculus has two halves that look unrelated. The fundamental theorem reveals they are inverses — the same way logarithm and exponential are inverses. This unification is the most powerful idea in elementary mathematics.

items.title: If a stock falls 50% then rises 50%, you've LOST money
items.claim: Stock at 100. Falls 50%: now 50. Rises 50%: now 75. Two equal-percentage moves in opposite directions don't cancel.

options.text: Percentages are RATIOS, not amounts. The 50% drop reduces the base; the subsequent 50% rise is on a smaller base. To recover from a -50% loss you need a +100% gain

items.reveal:
To go from x to y, percentage change is (y - x) / x.

Loss of L percent: new value = old * (1 - L/100).
Gain of G percent: new value = old * (1 + G/100).

For symmetric percent moves NOT to cancel, multiply: (1 - 0.5)(1 + 0.5) = 0.75. Always less than 1 if the magnitude is the same.

Recovery table:
- Lose 10%: need 11.1% to recover.
- Lose 25%: need 33.3% to recover.
- Lose 50%: need 100% to recover.
- Lose 75%: need 300% to recover.
- Lose 90%: need 900% to recover.

Applications:
- Drawdowns in investing: deep losses require enormous gains to recover. A 50% bear market loss takes years of strong returns to break even.
- Discounted prices then surcharged: 50% off followed by 50% on actually leaves you at 75% of original price (consumer gets a deal).
- Inflation: 10% inflation for 7 years halves purchasing power, even though 70% < 100%.

Geometric vs arithmetic mean: a stock returning +50%, -50%, +50%, -50% has arithmetic mean return 0% but geometric (actual) mean of ((1.5 * 0.5 * 1.5 * 0.5)^0.25 - 1) = -13.4%/period.
items.why: Percentages feel symmetric. They're multiplicative ratios that don't cancel directly. Anyone interpreting investment returns, weight changes, price comparisons or compound growth without realising this misreads the data.
